question: A 28-year-old shepherd from a rural cattle-rearing area presents with a large cystic liver lesion detected on ultrasound. He is afebrile and the lesion is echo-free with internal daughter cysts visible. Serology for Echinococcus is positive. The safest initial management is:

answers.text: Immediate image-guided percutaneous aspiration and drainage to confirm and drain the cyst

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Percutaneous aspiration of hydatid cysts risks anaphylaxis from leakage of scolices and daughter cysts, causing dissemination of disease. This is contraindicated as initial management — PAIR (puncture-aspiration-injection-reaspiration) requires specialist settings with pre-treatment albendazole.

answers.text: Albendazole pre-treatment followed by surgical cystectomy (or PAIR in selected cases) — treating hydatid cyst as hydatid until proven otherwise

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The rule is: any cystic liver lesion in an endemic area is hydatid until proven otherwise. Albendazole pre-treatment (at least 4 weeks) reduces viable scolices before surgical or PAIR intervention, preventing anaphylaxis and dissemination.

answers.text: IV metronidazole alone — the treatment of choice for amoebic liver abscess which also presents as a liver cyst in young adults

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Metronidazole treats amoebic liver abscesses, which are typically solitary, tender, and associated with diarrhoea. This patient has daughter cysts on ultrasound and positive Echinococcus serology — confirming hydatid disease, not amoebic abscess.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key rule: cystic liver lesion in endemic area = hydatid until disproven. The danger is blind aspiration causing anaphylaxis/dissemination. Albendazole pre-treatment is mandatory before any intervention.
Correct. Hydatid cyst in endemic area: albendazole pre-treatment → surgical/PAIR. NEVER aspirate without proper preparation — anaphylaxis risk is real.
